The existence of free will is crucial in understanding responsibility and accountability in society. Legal systems, moral standards, and social contracts are based on the assumption that humans have the ability to choose their actions. Without free will, the concepts of right and wrong become meaningless, as individuals would not be able to choose between them.
Some neurologists argue that our actions are initiated before we consciously become aware of them, suggesting that free will does not exist. This argument primarily addresses reactionary actions that occur in high-stress or time-sensitive situations, where individuals act based on ingrained habits or instincts. While this might be true in some cases, it does not invalidate the concept of free will. Over time, habits can solidify, but we are still responsible for cultivating these reactions and for choosing whether to act upon them.
Not all actions are reactionary. In many situations, we have ample time to reflect and make decisions based on reason, rather than reflex. This capacity to deliberate and choose is what distinguishes human behavior from mere instinct or reaction. Therefore, while certain actions may be automatic, we maintain the power and responsibility to shape our actions and, by extension, our inner selves (the Nafs) over time.
Conclusion
In both the physical and psychological realms, fixed laws guide outcomes. While free will introduces complexity into the system, it does not exempt individuals from responsibility for their actions. The laws governing the Nafs emphasize the importance of nurturing good qualities while avoiding those actions that degrade the soul. Ultimately, the choices we make shape not only our inner selves but also the broader fabric of society.

title: Inherited Religion
text:
Across the globe, humanity’s beliefs span a vast and fascinating spectrum:

Over a billion Hindus find deep spiritual connection through stone idols.
Approximately two-and-a-half billion Christians believe in the divine birth of God’s Son through a virgin.
One billion atheists firmly hold the conviction that no deity exists.
Among the two billion Muslims, whose holy book emphasizes justice, freedom, honesty, humanity, and peace, it is rare to find individuals practicing these principles with complete conviction.
The remaining global population, equally diverse in thought, holds an array of beliefs and philosophies.


In numerical terms, one billion equals 1,000,000,000 - a humbling reminder of the scale of our world. No matter your alignment with any particular -ism or non-ism, your beliefs will place you in a minority relative to the planet’s population, which is estimated to be more than 8 billions in 2024._

For instance, if you are Muslim, non-Muslims outnumber you by a ratio of nearly 3 to 1. Similarly, Christians find themselves in a comparable minority. Yet, these numbers carry no intrinsic validation or refutation of any belief system. Truth is not determined by majority rule.
An affinity with a religion, ethnicity, or place of origin does not determine one’s capacity to distinguish right from a wrong. History is witness to the fact that individuals from all walks of life have made profound contributions to science, knowledge, and intellectual discourse. While people from all walks of life make irrational decisions quite frequently.


Most individuals inherit their beliefs from their families and communities, seldom pausing to critically evaluate them. Take Christians, for example: their faith is often shaped by upbringing rather than a conscious, rational choice. Children are introduced to religious practices—attending church, listening to clergy, and absorbing teachings that eventually become internalized as personal truths.
Those who dare to question these handed-down beliefs are frequently labeled heretics or non-believers, a pattern not unique to Christianity but common across religions and traditions.
This phenomenon extends beyond religion. Many cling to inherited ideologies, rarely subjecting them to scrutiny. The result is a form of intellectual stagnation, where critical thinking is sidelined by blind adherence.



When individuals deviate from inherited beliefs, it often occurs subconsciously and is influenced by personal desires. Atheists, for instance, may reject religion due to perceived irrationalities but might not fully explore alternative perspectives. The decision to abandon religion can be driven by a desire to escape certain restrictions, yet this may come at the cost of overlooking valuable insights.
Beliefs, whether religious or secular, often serve self-serving interests. Even when science debunks misconceptions, it cannot definitively disprove the existence of a higher power, leaving room for an unbiased interpretation regarding a higher being. Yet, some reject - the notion of a higher being - driven by their personal desires alone.


Herd mentality - the tendency to adopt the beliefs and customs of one’s surroundings without critical examination - pervades human behavior. This mindset stifles individualism and discourages personal reflection.
For example, consider Michael, a devout Christian, grappling with religious dogma that contradicts his reasoning:
Michael Perspective:

“How can my parents, priests, and countless Christians, including scholars and intellectuals, all be wrong? Surely, someone among them has verified the truth of our beliefs … right?”

Diana’s Perspective: Michael’s younger sister, Diana, shares similar doubts but she resolves them differently:

“My doubts must stem from my own misunderstandings and intellectual limitations. How could my family and the multitude of Christians worldwide be mistaken?”

Michael and Diana’s Parents Perspective: Their parents echo this sentiment, relying on the sheer number of believers across generations as validation of their faith.

“How could such a vast multitude of believers, spanning across different generations and diverse backgrounds, be mistaken? It seems implausible for so many individuals to coalesce around a single belief system that is fundamentally flawed or entirely fictional!”

This pattern of thinking, whereby individuals rely on the beliefs and opinions of those around them instead of engaging in personal reflection and evaluation, epitomizes the essence of herd mentality.
Breaking free requires courage and introspection but rewards individuals with clarity, independence, and the ability to make informed choices.
Note: The choice of using Christian characters is arbitrary, which can be replaced with the choice of selecting any other religion.
The Role of Religious Scholars:
Even religious scholars, regarded as authorities, are not immune to this phenomenon. They often defer to the conclusions of past scholars, assuming their infallibility while acknowledging that current thinkers can err. Faith, they admit, sometimes requires a leap beyond intellectual reasoning — a reliance on blind faith.
The blind followers say:

@q-trans-en … Indeed, we found our (pious) fathers upon a religion and indeed we are in their footsteps (rightly) guided! @ref{Quran 43:22}


@q-trans-en … they say, “Good enough for us is that upon which we found our fathers..” @ref{Quran 5:104}

While God says:

@q-trans-en … “(such blind followers are) deaf, dumb, and blind, so they do not use their intellect.” @ref{Quran 2:171}





Herd mentality can ensnare even the most earnest individuals, discouraging critical thinking and personal exploration of deeply held beliefs. To transcend this, we must embrace courage, question inherited traditions, and strive for personal truths. In doing so, we liberate ourselves from the constraints of collective conformity and pave the way for genuine understanding and informed decision-making.

title: Intellectual Blindness
Intellectual Blindness
text:
Metaphors in the Quran serve as powerful tools, weaving vivid illustrations that resonate deeply with readers and transcend the boundaries of time and language.
One such metaphor is ‘blindness’, symbolizing a state where individuals abandon reason and logic, allowing desires and emotions to dictate their decisions. This often leads to the unquestioning acceptance of unverified dogmas and baseless beliefs, blinding individuals to the pursuit of truth and enlightenment.
Similarly, the Quran employs ‘death’ as a metaphor to represent stagnation and decay, whether in individuals or entire societies. It depicts a condition where, despite physical existence, there is a lack of responsiveness to truth and constructive dialogue—akin to speaking to the lifeless. This metaphor underscores the need for transformative change, urging a shift towards a vibrant, purposeful, and progressive way of life.
The Quran’s masterful use of such metaphors enables it to communicate profound truths in a memorable and engaging way. By eschewing overly technical language, it appeals directly to both the intellect and the soul, making its messages accessible to people across diverse backgrounds.
This is articulated clearly in the Quran:
@q-trans-en [Intellectually] blind and the seeing are not equal. Nor are the darknesses and the light … And the living and the dead are not alike … @ref{Quran 35:19-22}
Here, the Quran eloquently casts itself as ‘the light’ - a luminous guide for those seeking truth and enlightenment. In contrast, everything outside its teachings is portrayed as ‘darkness’. The capacity for reasoning and intellectual inquiry is celebrated as “seeing,” while the obstinate clinging to irrational beliefs is described as “blindness.” These metaphors emphasize the essential role of reason and critical thinking in the pursuit of knowledge and understanding.
Much like navigating in pitch darkness requires light, true guidance depends on two essential elements: the Quran as the source of enlightenment (the light) and intellectual reasoning (the seeing eyes) as the means to perceive it.

Just as light holds no value without one’s ability to see, the Quran’s teachings cannot be fully grasped or applied without a discerning and reflective mind.

Country of the Blind
text:
@lead Long ago, a hiker lost his footing and tumbled down a mountainside, landing in a hidden valley. Centuries before, a powerful earthquake had sealed this valley off from the rest of the world with massive rocks. While outsiders believed the inhabitants had perished, the truth was quite the opposite—they survived and even flourished in their secluded haven.
Not long after the earthquake, a genetic eye disease began to spread through the isolated community. Over time, it rendered each new generation blind from birth. Facing an uncertain future, the elders of the valley dedicated themselves to crafting ingenious methods to adapt and thrive in a world devoid of sight. As centuries passed, the memory of sight itself faded into myth, and the community came to believe that blindness was the natural order of life.
When the hiker regained consciousness and surveyed his surroundings, he realized he was in what could only be described as a “Country of the Blind.” Seeing himself as the proverbial “one-eyed king,” he tried to share his knowledge of the world as perceived through sight. Yet his efforts were met with confusion. The community struggled to grasp his descriptions of birdsong’s source, the sun’s warmth, or the stars’ glittering beauty. These wonders, tied to sight, were incomprehensible to them.
To the valley’s inhabitants, the hiker was not a beacon of wisdom but an anomaly. They had honed their other senses—smell, touch, and hearing — to extraordinary levels and regarded his clumsiness as a significant flaw. His reliance on sight seemed to them a peculiar deficiency, and his attempts to describe the world clashed with their deeply rooted beliefs about their visionless reality.
Over time, their patience waned. The hiker’s constant challenges to their worldview made him an outsider in more ways than one. Declared a heretic, he was ordered to leave. But with no way out of the sealed valley, the elders allowed him to stay—on the condition that he abandon all talk of sight.
Reluctantly, the man complied. However, as he grew to love a young woman in the community, he felt compelled to reveal to her the value of sight. His efforts, however well-intentioned, alarmed the woman, who reported them to the elders. After consulting the village doctor, they reached a chilling conclusion: the man’s “sight” was a peculiar malady, causing mental anguish and irrational claims.
The doctor proposed a cure: the removal of the man’s eyes. Stripping him of sight, they reasoned, would free him from his delusions and integrate him fully into their way of life. Faced with this ultimatum, the man was forced to confront a harrowing choice—conform to their world or cling to his vision.


In ‘The Country of the Blind’ by H. G. Wells, blindness serves as a metaphor for closed-mindedness, symbolizing societies resistant to new ideas and unwilling to question long-held beliefs. The valley becomes an allegory for insular communities that view inherited traditions as immutable truths, rejecting challenges and branding critical thinking as heresy.
In literature, blindness often represents intellectual stagnation, a failure to employ one’s cognitive faculties. Conversely, metaphorical “death” can signify willful indifference—ignoring efforts to awaken awareness or spark change. It embodies the dismissive refrain, “I don’t care,” and the willful rejection of growth.
This timeless narrative challenges us to examine the tension between innovation and tradition, the cost of conformity, and the courage it takes to see - and seek - a broader truth.

title: A Critique of Intellect
section: “Islamic Empire” and the Renaissance of Europe
text:
“Islamic Empire” and the Renaissance of Europe
The initial policies of the Islamic empire were supportive of reason-based thinking. Therefore, scientific learning and scholarship flourished throughout the empire. The conducive environment produced thousands of polymaths (scientists and scholars) during the first few hundred years.
A small list of Muslim mathematicians, astronomers, biologists, chemists, psychologists, economists, geographers, and philosophers, who were at the top of their fields in the entire world of their time, can be found on the Internet.
Al-gebra and al-gorithm are two of the most common phrases in mathematical and computer sciences, which bear the name of Muslim scientists born a thousand years ago — Geber (Jabir Bin Hayyan جابر بن حیّان ) died in 816 A.D. and Algorithmi (Al-Khwarizmi الخوارزمی ) died in 850 A.D., respectively. Whenever you see ‘al’ at the beginning of a scientific or scholarly term, chances are that it is a twisted form of an Arabic word. Hazen (Ibn al-Haytham ابن الہیثم ), Alberonius (Al-Bairuni البیرونی ) and Avicenna (Ibn-Sina ابن سینا ) were among the intellectuals whose works have survived to date, to some degree.
Although most of the original work from that era has been lost to history, it served as a steppingstone for the European Renaissance scholars and scientists. To build the scientific foundation, Europe was already translating and studying the writings of Muslim scholars by the end of the 11th century.

title: A Critique of Intellect

text:
Al-Ghazali — The Intellect Slayer
It is said that after Al-Ghazali [1058 – 1111 A.D.] criticized the scientific approach in his landmark book, ‘Tahafat-ul-Filasafa’ [ تہافت الفلاسفة ] — ‘The Incoherence of the Scientists’, the spirit of scientific inquiry died in the Muslim lands. (Recall why scientists and scientific methods are being challenged by faith-based organizations and individuals in the U.S.A. today.)
Imam Ghazali [ امام غزالی ] begins his book with the allegations against Muslim scientists as follows:

“I have observed that there is a class of people who believe in… intelligence and insight. They have abandoned all religious rituals.. and defy the injunctions of Shariah (ritualistic laws)… for they were born into an un-Islamic atmosphere and their parents were not any better …”

Imam Ghazali continues …

“[they believe] that the mathematical, logical, physical and metaphysical sciences … are the most profound; that their excellent intelligence justifies their bold attempts to discover the Hidden Things (laws of nature via causes-and-effects); and that with … their intelligence and … accomplishments, they reject the authority of shariah laws … and believe that all such things are only sacred lies (lies in the name of sacred people) and (thus) nonsense. … They refused to be content with the religion followed by their ancestors …” (Ghazali)

If the above quoted statements ring a bell, it is not a surprise. Recall ‘The Country of The Blind’. These are the same allegations that religious scholars use against those who prefer reason to blind faith.
Imam Ghazali deals with many issues in the book, but I will go with the most fundamental topic in natural sciences that Imam Ghazali attacked: the law of cause-and-effect, which is the basis for all natural sciences.
Note: There was no separation of, or distinction between scientists and philosophers in older times. There was no separate word for a scientist; they were called philosophers. You can safely replace the word ‘philosopher’ with ‘scientist-philosopher’ when you read an older book.

The Cause-and-Effect
It was well-established among Muslim scientists that things do not depart from their natural course. If there is a cause, the effect will follow. Everything in this world follows this principle. To refute this claim, Imam Ghazali writes:

“The connection between the cause and the effect is not necessary … Take for instance any two things … burning and contact with fire; light and the rise of the Sun; death and the severance of the head from the trunk (none is due to cause and effect.) …”
“[Scientists] claim that fire is an agent of burning and whenever there is fire, it cannot stop from doing what is in its nature to do (i.e., burn) after it comes into contact with a subject.”

Imam Ghazali further explains that when you show fire to cotton, cotton turns black and disintegrates. But how can [science] claim that fire burned it? Fire does not burn the cotton; it is God who turns the cotton black and disintegrates it. God does this either by Himself or through His angels. Fire is an inanimate thing; it has no power (of its own) to burn other things. [Scientists] only see the fire coming closer to the cotton and then cotton turning black, but it is God (and not the fire) who (burns and) turns cotton black.
The argument presented here is a good argument, but I do not know how it can be twisted to deduce what has been claimed in the preface of his book? Imam Ghazali gives his own reasons.
For Imam Ghazali, there are no Hidden Secrets of nature (natural laws). It is always God Who is active in His World. He does whatever He Wills! He acts according to His Wishes. Since He wishes that cotton must burn whenever fire comes closer, He turns the cotton black.
In other words, believers in cause-and-effect start believing that fire has an inherent power to burn cotton; and thus, God is not needed. This is a violation of Islamic theology according to Imam Ghazali and all subsequent Muslim scholars.

Where Did Imam Ghazali Fail?
Imam Ghazali wanted to keep the door for miracles open, but he forgot that the Quran offers a reason-based message.

title: An Unpredictable World
text:
The question of where we come from is complex and multi-faceted. To truly understand the origins of humanity, we would need a time machine to take us back to the very beginning of everything. In my imagination, I stumbled upon such a device.
The time machine transported me to a world I call the “Puniverse”—a term I coined to represent the pre-Big Bang universe. This world was eerily similar to our own, complete with a sun, moon, stars, and earth. However, upon closer inspection, I began to notice peculiarities that I couldn’t quite comprehend.
For example, the sun did not rise from the east every day as we expect, but instead, its rising point changed unpredictably. Rivers flowed in unexpected directions, and other natural phenomena seemed alien to me. It became apparent that the immutable laws of physics we take for granted in our world were not fixed in the Puniverse; instead, they changed at random.
On one occasion, I encountered Pewton sitting under an apple tree. But unlike our universe, no apple fell on his head. Some apples fell to the ground, while others flew off in random directions. Pewton was unable to discover any laws, including the law of gravity, due to the lack of consistency in the Puniverse. Without predictability, there was no way to invent machines, aircraft, rockets, or other tools.

title: An Unpredictable World
text:
Unpredictable God
One bright day, when the sun arose from the west, a messenger arrived with a revelation from God:

“I am your Lord and the Creator of everything.”
“I am the Almighty and I do whatever I feel like doing. I have the power to make the sun rise from the east and the west, to make rivers flow down and up the hill, to make apples fly off the tree, and to create children from virgins.”
“See for yourself! I twist natural laws, whenever I Will, to show you miracles and my Power. I am a Living God [and not a dead watch-maker] So, will you not accept My control over your world? If you do so, you will get an absolute peace of mind [by not wasting your energies in search of fixed natural laws.]”

title: An Unpredictable World
text:
Unpredictable Nonbelievers
The capricious Will of the Almighty was the obvious driving force behind everything in the Puniverse, yet hardly anyone believed in the message. And why should they?
There was no universal pattern to be found. It seemed as though multiple gods were fighting with each other over how to run the daily affairs of the world. Some gods wanted the sun to rise from the east, while others preferred it to rise from the west. Some gods wanted rivers to flow uphill, while others wanted them to flow downhill. There was no single, powerful hand to keep things consistent!
Or perhaps, there was One Powerful God who had fallen into a deep slumber, and things were going haywire on their own.
Perhaps, the One Powerful God was awake but suffering from episodes of ‘confidence crises’ or ‘mood swings.’ Did He need to show miracles to prove His power and control over everything?

title: An Unpredictable World
text:
Our Sweet Predictable World
We are fortunate to live in a world where the laws of nature are predictable. Newton and Einstein were born in a universe where all things follow consistent patterns that can be discovered. From black holes and stars to atoms and quarks, everything is bound by universal laws. One powerful and wise God has created these laws and controls everything in the universe. His will is unwavering and indomitable!

title: An Unpredictable World
text:
Predictable Nonbelievers
People look at the universe and see fixed, consistent natural laws. They take these laws for granted and wonder why God doesn’t show us miracles to prove His existence and power.
Religious people rise to this challenge and proudly claim miraculous stories from their sacred texts. Unaware of the Puniverse, many of us blindly fall prey to these religious fairy tales. But why are we so inclined to believe such myths? The answer can be summarized in two short paragraphs:
The powerful forces of nature instilled fear in primitive humans. Acknowledging their own helplessness against these forces, they sought to appease the unknown controller of these forces through sacrifices and worship. Depraved priesthoods, capricious kings, and corrupt elites incessantly exploited these fearful humans, who lacked self-confidence.
The long history of exploitation has scarred the human subconscious to the point where the idea of a law-abiding God feels alien, if not repulsive. The mental image of a God who does not show miracles diminishes the awe of a powerful, mighty “Superman.”
The universe reveals its grandeur and splendor, but how can humans trust its Creator unless He demonstrates His “real” power by breaking the very rules He set for the universe?
“Who will believe in a God who does not part the Red Sea for Moses, does not make Mary conceive Jesus without a spouse, or does not teleport Muhammad to Jerusalem and back overnight?” wonders the fearful primitive man, lacking confidence.
We focus on what we want to see in God, rather than what God wants us to see through His Creation — the Universe that operates according to His rules (natural laws) in His Kingdom (the physical world).
Sadly, the primitive mind still yearns for a Macho Being in the guise of a God!
Some say, “God created man in His own image.” I would respond, “Men created God in their own images!”

title: The God of Miracles
text:
The God of Miracles
What is a miracle? It is an event that violates natural laws — such as a person walking on water without sinking, or emerging from a fire unscathed. If a natural cause can be found for the event, it cannot be considered a miracle. For instance, if a person walks on a water surface that is frozen to ice, it is not a miracle; it’s simply the result of natural laws.
Now, take a moment to reflect on the following questions:

@maroon Will you stop believing in God if He stops performing miracles?

Who, in your view, created the natural (physical) laws? Remember, scientists do not create these laws — they merely discover them. They observe patterns in nature and describe them using scientific language or notations. Descriptions of natural phenomena are what we call natural laws.
With these thoughts in mind, let’s revisit the earlier question:

Consider a sharpshooter aiming at a deer in the woods. If the sharpshooter doesn’t fire and lets the deer escape, would you question their ability to shoot, or would you wonder why they didn’t take the shot?
If God created everything, His ability to manipulate nature is not in question. The real question isn’t about “if” or “when,” but rather “why.” Why would He alter the natural course of the universe to perform miracles? Would it not be unfair to those who were not present to witness the miracle firsthand? Why should they rely solely on hearsay?
Furthermore, a miracle does not prove anything. Even if you observe a miracle firsthand, how can you objectively distinguish between a genuine miracle and a magician’s trick? The line between the two can be incredibly thin. In addition, how can a description of a miracle by hearsay be any evidence of truth for others!
Now, consider an athlete who starts her daily exercise routine at 5 a.m. Would you view her as a slave to the clock, or as someone admirable for her consistency and punctuality?
Why do you think God’s Will is in question if He chooses not to break the laws He established for the universe to follow? A strong will isn’t one that bends under pressure. God’s Will is the strongest — it does not falter. He has the absolute power to execute His Will, consistently causing apples to fall to the ground, time and time again.
Consider a schoolteacher. Should the teacher treat all students equally according to a fair set of rules, or should they favor students based on personal feelings? For example, should they pass students who flatter them while failing those who work hard and score full marks but never praise the teacher?
If all humans are equal before God, what else would you expect from Him? Everyone will reap what they sow. Good deeds are rewarded, and wrongdoings are repaid. These are the fairest rules set by God. Flattery may deceive humans, but it does not deceive God, Who is all-Knowing, all-Seeing, and Just.
The beauty of God’s consistent Will is that all are treated equally—no one can claim unfairness. Fire does not get to choose when or whom to burn. Likewise, God’s plan is flawless, requiring no intervention to fix any perceived imperfections.
